maternal obesity is a risk factor for neonatal admission but not necessarily for severe fetal impairment.

maternal BMI is associated with maternal and fetal pregnancy outcomes and with the outcome of newborns admitted to a neonate care unit.

the impact of maternal body mass on fetal and neonatal outcome.
the question of how maternal body mass index affects fetal outcome.
the question of whether the increased risk for admission to a neonatal unit in children from obese women is a consequence of the maternal obesity or a result of fetal complications.

maternal body mass index is associated with maternal and fetal complications, and that the neonatal outcome of children from obese mothers is not necessarily worse compared to children from mothers of normal body mass index.
the impact of maternal obesity on pregnancy outcome is heterogeneous.
maternal obesity is associated with increased incidence of hypertensive complications, macrosomia and fetal hypoglycemia.

the risk of neonatal morbidity is lowest in children from normal weight women and highest in children from underweight women.
the impact of maternal body mass is not uniform and depends on the BMI range.
the neonate from a healthy weight mother has the best outcome and the neonate from an obese mother the second best outcome.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the increased risk of neonatal admission in the children from obese mothers is due to the increased risk of macrosomia, and that the neonates from obese mothers do not exhibit a worse outcome in comparison to neonates from healthy weight mothers.
